concepts.title: Tokens, Tokenization, and Context Windows
concepts.description: Every LLM operates over tokens, not words or characters -- and the context window's fixed token budget, shared between everything you send in and everything the model writes back, is the single most consequential constraint on what you can build with it.
learningObjectives: Explain why LLMs operate on subword tokens rather than characters or whole words, and what problem that design solves.
Describe roughly how byte-pair-style tokenization splits text, and predict which kinds of text will tokenize efficiently versus poorly.
Explain what a context window is, what counts against it, and what happens when a request exceeds it.
Identify the practical consequences of a finite context window: per-token cost, latency, and the 'lost in the middle' attention effect.
Choose an appropriate strategy -- truncation, chunking, summarization, or retrieval -- when input doesn't fit in the available budget.

sections.heading: Why Tokens, Not Characters or Words
sections.body:
Every LLM you'll integrate with -- via an API, a local weights file, whatever -- consumes and produces sequences of **tokens**, not characters and not whole words. That's a deliberate engineering compromise, and understanding why it was chosen tells you a lot about how the model actually behaves.

If a model operated on individual characters, sequences would become very long very fast (an average English sentence is roughly 5x more characters than words), which matters because the computational cost of the attention mechanism inside a transformer grows faster than linearly with sequence length -- doubling the sequence length more than doubles the compute. Character-level models also have to learn spelling and morphology essentially from scratch, spending model capacity on something a slightly larger unit would give for free.

If a model operated on whole words instead, you'd hit the opposite problem: an open vocabulary. Human language mints new words constantly -- product names, typos, code identifiers, someone's username, words in dozens of languages -- and a fixed word-level vocabulary either explodes to millions of entries or has to map every unfamiliar word to a generic 'unknown' placeholder, throwing away information the model badly needs.

Subword tokenization is the compromise that avoids both failure modes: common whole words become single tokens (fast, cheap, and the model has seen them a billion times), while rare or novel words get decomposed into smaller, recurring subword pieces the model has also seen many times, just recombined differently. No token is ever truly 'unknown' -- worst case, an unfamiliar string gets broken all the way down to individual bytes, so the model can still represent absolutely any input, it just costs more tokens to do it.

sections.heading: How Byte-Pair-Style Tokenization Actually Splits Text
sections.body:
The dominant family of tokenizers used in production LLMs is built on **byte-pair encoding (BPE)** or close variants of it. The vocabulary isn't hand-designed; it's learned from a large text corpus, offline, before the model itself is ever trained: start with every individual byte as its own token, then repeatedly find the most frequently-occurring adjacent pair of tokens in the corpus and merge that pair into a single new token, added to the vocabulary. Repeat that merge step tens of thousands of times and you end up with a vocabulary -- typically on the order of 50,000 to 200,000 entries depending on the model family -- that contains everything from single characters up through entire common words and even common short phrases.

The practical upshot is a set of patterns worth internalizing: common English words ('the', 'is', 'running') are usually a single token. Less common words, technical jargon, and words in morphologically rich languages often split into two or three tokens ('tokenization' might become something like 'token' + 'ization'). Whitespace, punctuation, and capitalization typically affect where boundaries fall -- ' Hello' (with a leading space) and 'Hello' (without one) are frequently two entirely different tokens, not the same token with a flag. Numbers and random-looking strings (UUIDs, hashes, hex-encoded data) tokenize especially poorly, often close to one token per character or per few characters, because the merge process never saw enough repetition in those strings to justify building bigger merged tokens for them.

This has a very concrete consequence for anyone building on top of these models: a block of JSON with long random IDs, or a paragraph of a language underrepresented in the training corpus, can consume several times more tokens than an equal-length paragraph of plain English -- which matters directly for both cost and how much of your context budget it eats.

sections.heading: The Context Window: One Shared, Fixed Budget
sections.body:
The **context window** is the maximum number of tokens a model can attend to in a single call -- and critically, it is one shared pool, not separate pools for input and output. Your system prompt, conversation history, any documents you paste or retrieve, the user's actual question, and the model's own generated response all draw from the exact same token budget. A model with, say, a 128,000-token context window doesn't give you 128,000 tokens of input *plus* however much output you want -- if your input consumes 127,900 tokens, you have roughly 100 tokens left for the entire response, no matter how large the window nominally is.

When a request's token count -- input alone, or input plus the requested maximum output length -- exceeds what the model supports, you don't get a degraded or partial response; you typically get an outright API error (something like a context-length-exceeded error) or, in some client libraries, silent truncation of the oldest content, which is arguably worse because it fails without telling you. Either way, this is not a soft limit you can lean against -- it's a hard wall that shows up as a production incident the first time a user pastes in something unusually long.

It's also worth being precise about what 'context window' does and doesn't promise. A large context window means the model *can* mathematically attend to that many tokens. It says nothing about whether the model will use every part of that window equally well -- which is exactly the subject of the next section.

sections.heading: Practical Consequences: Cost, Latency, and Lost-in-the-Middle
sections.body:
Three practical effects follow directly from the fact that everything is measured, and paid for, in tokens. First, **cost scales with tokens**, typically at different per-token rates for input versus output -- a feature that processes long documents will cost noticeably more per call than one that processes short chat turns, and this is usually the single biggest lever for controlling LLM spend at scale, well before you start optimizing prompts for quality. Second, **latency scales with total tokens processed** -- both how much you send and how much you ask the model to generate -- so a chatty system prompt repeated on every single call, or an unnecessarily long requested output, has a real, measurable effect on how snappy your feature feels.

Third, and less obvious: models do not attend to every position in a long context with equal effectiveness. Empirically and in practice, models tend to make best use of information near the very start and the very end of the context, with a measurable dip in retrieval accuracy for facts placed deep in the middle of a long input -- an effect commonly called **'lost in the middle.'** This means simply cramming more relevant material into the context window is not a free win even when it technically fits within the token budget; a shorter, well-curated context that puts the most important information near the edges of the prompt can genuinely outperform a longer one that buries it in the center.

Taken together, these three effects mean context window size is a budget to spend deliberately, not a resource to maximize by default -- the goal is almost always 'the smallest context that reliably contains what's actually needed,' not 'as much as will fit.'

sections.heading: Strategies When Your Input Doesn't Fit
sections.body: When the material you want the model to see is larger than the available budget, you have a small number of real options, each with different tradeoffs. **Truncation** -- simply cutting off content past some length -- is the cheapest to implement and the riskiest: you're gambling that whatever gets cut wasn't important, with no principled way to know. **Chunking and processing separately** (sometimes called a map-reduce pattern) splits the input into pieces that each fit comfortably, processes each piece independently (say, summarizing each chunk of a long document), then combines those intermediate results, possibly with another pass over the combined summaries -- this scales to arbitrarily large inputs but costs more total tokens and more calls, and can lose cross-chunk context that spans a boundary. **Summarization as compression** shrinks earlier content (like older turns of a long conversation) into a denser summary before it's fed forward again, trading some fidelity for a smaller footprint. And **retrieval** -- covered in full in the next module -- sidesteps the problem differently: instead of trying to fit everything, you select only the subset of available material that's actually relevant to the current request and feed in just that. In production systems, retrieval is usually the default answer to 'my knowledge base is bigger than the context window,' while chunking/summarization tend to be the answer to 'this one specific input is bigger than the context window.'

examples.title: Counting Tokens Before You Call the API
examples.code:
import tiktoken

encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

english = "The quarterly report is due on Friday."
random_ids = "a3f9c2-8b1e-4d7a-91c0-f2e6b7d1a9c4"

print(len(encoding.encode(english)))      # around 8 tokens
print(len(encoding.encode(random_ids)))   # around 20+ tokens, despite being a similar length string
examples.explanation: Both strings are roughly the same character length, but they tokenize wildly differently, and the reason is entirely about repetition in the training corpus the tokenizer was built from. 'quarterly report is due on Friday' is made of common English words and word-fragments that appeared constantly during BPE merge-learning, so each maps to one or two tokens. The hex/UUID-like string almost never appeared as repeated substrings during that same process -- there's no reason a merge step would ever have combined 'a3f' into one token, because that exact substring is essentially random -- so the tokenizer falls back to much smaller pieces, close to a token every couple of characters. This is exactly why logs, IDs, hashes, and other structured-but-unnatural text quietly blow through token budgets and cost far more than their character count suggests; checking with the actual tokenizer before you ship, rather than estimating by character or word count, is the only reliable way to know.

examples.title: Watching Rare Words Split Into Subword Pieces
examples.code:
import tiktoken

encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

for word in ["the", "tokenization", "antidisestablishmentarianism"]:
    token_ids = encoding.encode(word)
    pieces = [encoding.decode([t]) for t in token_ids]
    print(word, "->", pieces)

# 'the' -> ['the']                                   (1 token: extremely common)
# 'tokenization' -> ['token', 'ization']              (2 tokens: common word + common suffix)
# 'antidisestablishmentarianism' -> multiple fragments (5+ tokens: rare, decomposed further)
examples.explanation: The exact split points depend on the specific tokenizer and vocabulary a given model family uses, so treat the illustrative splits above as representative of the pattern rather than a guaranteed output for every tokenizer -- but the pattern itself is universal across BPE-family tokenizers. Extremely common words survive as a single token because the merge process had massive repeated evidence to justify building one token for them. A moderately common word built from a common root plus a common suffix splits into exactly those recognizable pieces, because 'token' and 'ization' both individually appeared often enough elsewhere to earn their own token, but 'tokenization' as a whole unit didn't appear often enough to earn a merge of its own. A genuinely rare word gets chopped into several smaller fragments, none of which look like meaningful sub-words to a human reader -- the tokenizer has no notion of morphology, only of statistical frequency in its training corpus. This is why domain-specific or jargon-heavy text (legal, medical, a codebase full of unusual identifier names) tends to consume noticeably more tokens per word than everyday prose.

examples.title: Hitting the Context Window Limit in a Chat Loop
examples.code:
conversation = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}]

def send_turn(user_text, call_model):
    conversation.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    reply = call_model(conversation)   # sends the ENTIRE history every single time
    conversation.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    return reply

# After enough turns, this raises something like:
# BadRequestError: This model's maximum context length is 128000 tokens.
# You requested 131204 tokens (128900 in the messages, 2304 in the completion).
examples.explanation: This is a genuinely common shape of bug in chatbot code: because the entire conversation history is resent on every single turn (which is necessary -- the model has no memory between calls, so anything it should 'remember' has to be re-sent), the token count of a single request grows every turn, monotonically, with no upper bound baked into the code. Nothing fails for a while, which is exactly what makes it dangerous -- it works fine in every quick manual test, and then fails in production during exactly the kind of long, engaged conversation you'd want to handle well. The error message itself is worth reading closely: it separately reports tokens used by the messages versus tokens reserved for the completion, which is the concrete proof that input and output share one combined budget. The fix is never 'just increase the limit' (you don't control the model's window) -- it's to actively manage the history: drop or summarize the oldest turns once the running total approaches some threshold below the actual maximum, leaving headroom for the response.

misconceptions.description: A token is roughly the same thing as a word, so you can estimate token counts by counting words.
misconceptions.clarification: For everyday English prose, a rough rule of thumb of about 4 characters or three-quarters of a word per token is a reasonable estimate -- but 'roughly the same as a word' badly breaks down for exactly the content that matters most in production systems: numbers, IDs, code, punctuation-heavy text, and non-English languages routinely tokenize at a much worse (higher tokens-per-character) ratio than plain English prose does. Relying on a word count to predict token count, and therefore cost or context-budget usage, will systematically underestimate for precisely the inputs most likely to be long or unusual -- the only reliable approach is to run the actual tokenizer for the model you're using.

misconceptions.description: A bigger context window means you should feed the model as much information as will technically fit, since more context can only help.
misconceptions.clarification: More context is not free and is not uniformly useful. It costs more money and more latency in direct proportion to the extra tokens, and empirically, models attend less reliably to information placed in the middle of a long context than to information near the start or end ('lost in the middle') -- so padding a prompt with marginally-relevant material can measurably degrade the quality of a response even when everything relevant is technically present somewhere in the window. The better default is to include only what's actually needed, positioned deliberately, rather than maximizing how much fits.

exercises.prompt: Two strings are roughly the same character length: a plain English sentence, and a string of randomly generated hexadecimal characters (like a hash). Both are passed through the same BPE-style tokenizer. Which one will produce more tokens, and roughly why?
exercises.code:
import tiktoken

encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

sentence = "Please review the attached document before Monday."
hex_string = "9f8a3c1e7b2d4f6a0c9e8b7d3f1a5c2e"

print(len(encoding.encode(sentence)))
print(len(encoding.encode(hex_string)))
hints: Tokenizer vocabularies are built by repeatedly merging the most FREQUENT adjacent pairs seen in a large training corpus -- not by any understanding of grammar or meaning.

Ask yourself: which of these two strings is more likely to contain substrings that recur constantly across a huge text corpus, and which is closer to random noise that never repeats in a learnable way?

Common English words and word-fragments earned single tokens because they appeared over and over during merge-learning. A random hex string, by construction, almost never repeats the same substring twice.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The hex string produces noticeably more tokens per character than the English sentence, even though both strings are a similar length. The sentence prints a small number of tokens (roughly 8-9), while the hex string prints a larger number (often close to one token per 2-3 characters).
exercises.solutionExplanation: The English sentence is built almost entirely from common words the tokenizer's vocabulary has dedicated single tokens for, because those words (and common word-fragments) appeared enormously often in whatever corpus was used to learn the BPE merges. The hex string, by contrast, is effectively random from the tokenizer's point of view -- there's no reason any particular sequence like '9f8a' would have appeared often enough, verbatim, elsewhere in the training corpus to justify merging it into its own token. So the tokenizer falls back to much smaller units for it, producing more tokens for the same number of characters. This is a direct, practical consequence of BPE being a frequency-driven, not a meaning-driven, process.

exercises.prompt: This chatbot function works fine in early testing but starts failing with a context-length error partway through long conversations. Find the underlying design bug and fix it so long conversations degrade gracefully instead of crashing.
exercises.code:
conversation = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}]

def send_turn(user_text, call_model):
    conversation.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    reply = call_model(conversation)
    conversation.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    return reply
hints: The entire `conversation` list is resent on every single call, and it only ever grows -- nothing ever removes or shrinks earlier turns.
Since input and output tokens share one fixed budget per call, a history that grows without bound will eventually leave no room for even a short reply.
You need a policy for what to do once the running conversation gets close to the model's limit -- consider dropping or summarizing the oldest turns while always keeping the system message.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug isn't a syntax error -- it's an architectural one: the code assumes conversation history can grow forever within a fixed-size budget, which is never true. The fix introduces an explicit token-budget check (`count_tokens`) and a trimming policy (`trim_history`) that runs before every call, removing the oldest non-system turns once the running total approaches a threshold safely below the model's actual maximum. Keeping the system message pinned at index 0 while trimming from index 1 onward preserves the assistant's core instructions even as older conversational turns are discarded. A more sophisticated version would summarize the dropped turns into a short recap rather than deleting them outright, but the trimming version already converts a hard crash into graceful, bounded degradation.

assessments.prompt: A context window is described as '128,000 tokens.' What does that number actually limit?
options: Only the text you send as input; the model's response doesn't count against it.
Only the model's response length; you can send as much input as you want.
The combined total of input tokens and output tokens for that single request.
The number of separate messages you can include in a conversation, regardless of their length.
assessments.explanation: The context window is one shared budget covering everything involved in a single call: system prompt, conversation history, any retrieved or pasted content, the user's message, and the tokens the model generates in response. Option A and option B each wrongly assume input and output are tracked separately with independent limits -- they aren't; consuming more on one side directly leaves less room on the other. Option D is wrong because the limit is fundamentally about total token count, not message count -- a single very long message can exceed the window on its own, and many short messages can too, once their tokens add up.

assessments.prompt: A teammate proposes building a document Q&A feature by concatenating the full text of up to 200 uploaded PDFs into a single prompt, reasoning that the model's context window is 'large enough' since the combined text fits under the token limit. Explain why this is likely to perform poorly even if it technically fits, and what you'd propose instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Fitting under the token limit is a necessary condition for this to work at all, but it's far from sufficient for it to work well. Three separate problems stack on top of each other. First, cost and latency scale directly with total tokens processed, and 200 full PDFs concatenated together is very likely tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens -- every single question the user asks would reprocess that entire mass of text from scratch, making the feature slow and expensive per query even if only a handful of sentences across those 200 documents actually contain the answer. Second, and more subtly, models don't attend to a long context uniformly -- the 'lost in the middle' effect means information buried deep within a huge concatenated blob is measurably less likely to be used correctly than information near the start or end, so relevant content from, say, document 140 out of 200 might get effectively ignored even though it's technically present in the prompt. Third, this approach doesn't scale -- the moment a 201st document is uploaded, or the total text creeps past the context window, the whole approach breaks outright with no graceful path forward. The better architecture is retrieval-augmented generation: index the documents ahead of time (chunk them and embed each chunk), and for each user question, retrieve only the small number of chunks that are actually relevant to that specific question, then include just those in the prompt. This keeps each individual call small, fast, and cheap regardless of how many documents are in the corpus, and it sidesteps the lost-in-the-middle problem by only ever including content that's likely to matter for the question at hand rather than everything at once.

assessments.prompt: A BPE-style tokenizer's vocabulary is built by starting with individual bytes and repeatedly merging pairs of tokens. Which pairs get merged, and why does that make a random hex string like 'a3f9c2e1' split into far more tokens than a common English phrase of similar length?
options: The most frequently co-occurring adjacent pairs in the training corpus get merged into new tokens; random hex characters rarely repeat the same substring, so no large merged token was ever created for them.
Pairs are merged in alphabetical order until the vocabulary reaches its target size, which happens to favor letters over digits.
The tokenizer merges pairs based on a hand-written list of common English morphemes, and hex digits were never added to that list.
Every character is merged with its immediate neighbor exactly once, regardless of frequency, so token count only depends on string length.
assessments.explanation: BPE vocabularies are learned, not designed: the training process repeatedly finds the most frequent adjacent pair of existing tokens across a large corpus and merges it into one new token, thousands of times over. Common English words and fragments earn big merged tokens because they recur constantly. A random-looking hex string almost never repeats the exact same substring anywhere in the corpus, so the merge process never had a statistical reason to build a larger token for it, leaving it to fall back to small, near-byte-level pieces. Options B, C, and D all describe mechanisms BPE does not use -- it is purely frequency-driven, with no alphabetical ordering, no hand-curated morpheme list, and no fixed one-merge-per-character rule.

assessments.prompt: You're assembling a prompt that includes several retrieved facts and a final user question, and only one fact can be flagged as the single most important one. Based on the 'lost in the middle' effect described in this module, where should that critical fact be placed to give the model the best chance of using it correctly?
options: Anywhere is equally fine, since a large enough context window guarantees uniform attention across all positions.
Buried in the exact middle of the context, since models focus attention on the center of long inputs.
Near the very start or the very end of the context, since models empirically attend less reliably to information placed deep in the middle of a long input.
Repeated ten times evenly spaced throughout the context, so at least one occurrence lands in an attended position.
assessments.explanation: The module describes 'lost in the middle' as a measurable dip in retrieval accuracy for facts placed deep in the middle of a long context, with models making comparatively better use of information near the start and end. Option A is wrong because a large context window only guarantees a fact mathematically fits, not that it's attended to equally well. Option B has the effect backwards. Option D isn't a strategy discussed in the module and adds unnecessary token cost rather than addressing the actual positional effect.

assessments.prompt: A production system needs to answer questions against a knowledge base of 50,000 support articles -- far larger than any model's context window could ever hold at once. Per the strategies discussed in this module, which approach is the best default fit for this specific situation, and why?
options: Truncation: send as many articles as fit and cut off the rest, since the model can usually infer the missing parts.
Chunking and map-reduce: split all 50,000 articles into pieces, summarize every piece for every question, then combine the summaries.
Retrieval: index the articles ahead of time and, for each question, select only the subset of articles actually relevant to it.
Summarization: compress all 50,000 articles into one dense summary once, and reuse that same summary for every future question.
assessments.explanation: The module explicitly distinguishes these strategies by scenario: retrieval is the default answer when the overall knowledge base is bigger than the context window, because it selects only the relevant subset per query rather than trying to process everything every time. Truncation risks silently cutting relevant articles with no way to know what was lost. Running full map-reduce summarization across all 50,000 articles for every single question is enormously wasteful compared to retrieving the handful of relevant ones. A single static summary of the entire knowledge base would lose the specific detail needed to answer most individual questions accurately -- summarization is better suited to compressing one specific oversized input, not standing in for a whole knowledge base.

concepts.title: Next-Token Prediction: How Generation Actually Works
concepts.description: An LLM writing a paragraph is not planning ahead, outlining, or reasoning in the way it appears to -- it is repeatedly computing a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary and picking one token at a time, each choice conditioned on everything written so far, including its own prior output.
learningObjectives: Describe the autoregressive generation loop: how a model produces a response one token at a time and what makes the loop stop.
Explain what logits and a softmax-derived probability distribution over the vocabulary represent at each generation step.
Explain why the model has no separate planning phase, and what that implies about both its coherence and its failure modes.
Explain why every previously generated token -- including the model's own output -- feeds back in as input to generating the next one.
Predict how changing a single earlier word in a prompt can cascade into a completely different completion.

sections.heading: The Generation Loop: One Token at a Time
sections.body:
Strip away everything else, and text generation from an LLM is a simple loop repeated many times: take the sequence of tokens seen so far (system prompt, conversation history, user message, and any tokens the model has already generated in this response), feed that whole sequence through the model in a single forward pass, get back a probability distribution over every possible next token, select one token from that distribution, append it to the sequence, and repeat -- now with a sequence one token longer than before.

The loop terminates for one of a small number of reasons: the model generates a special end-of-sequence token that it has learned marks 'the response is complete'; the response hits a maximum-length limit you configured; or the generated text matches a stop sequence you specified (a string that, once produced, should end generation immediately, often used to prevent the model from continuing past a clear boundary like the start of a new turn).

There is no other machinery involved beyond this loop. Whatever multi-paragraph structure, argument, or narrative a long response has, it was produced by this exact same single-token-at-a-time mechanism, run enough times in a row -- nothing about the mechanism changes for a one-word answer versus a ten-page report.

sections.heading: From Logits to Probabilities: What's Actually Computed
sections.body:
At each step of the loop, the model's final layer produces one real number, called a **logit**, for every single entry in its vocabulary -- tens of thousands of numbers, one per possible next token, representing (roughly) how strongly the model's learned parameters favor that token as the continuation given everything so far. Those raw logits are not probabilities themselves; a function called **softmax** converts them into a proper probability distribution -- a set of numbers between 0 and 1 that sum to exactly 1 across the whole vocabulary, where a larger logit becomes a larger probability.

The next token is then chosen from that distribution -- either deterministically (always the single highest-probability token, called greedy decoding) or by actually sampling according to the probabilities (which is where temperature and nucleus sampling come in, covered in depth in the next concept). Either way, the crucial thing to internalize here is that **there is no rule-based grammar, no lookup table, and no symbolic reasoning step choosing the next word** -- it is entirely the output of this learned probability distribution, produced by the same forward pass regardless of whether the 'right' next token is grammatically obvious ('the' after 'I went to') or genuinely uncertain (the next digit of a number the model is fabricating).

sections.heading: No Explicit Plan -- Yet Surprisingly Coherent
sections.body:
This is the detail that trips people up the most, because it cuts against how it feels to read a long, well-structured piece of model output: there is no separate 'decide the outline, then write the prose' phase happening anywhere in the mechanism described above. Every single token, including the very first word of a ten-paragraph essay, is generated by the exact same next-token-prediction step, conditioned only on the tokens that already exist.

How, then, does the output so often come out globally coherent rather than a word salad? The honest answer is that at the scale these models are trained -- vast amounts of text, enormous parameter counts -- the learned probability distribution itself has implicitly absorbed the patterns of what coherent, well-structured continuations look like. Predicting 'what word plausibly comes next in text like this' turns out, empirically, to require the model to represent something functionally very close to topic, tone, and intent internally, purely as a means of doing next-token prediction well -- not because anyone designed an explicit planning module.

This has real consequences for how you should think about failure modes. Because there's no separate correction phase, an early token that commits the response to a wrong path (a wrong number, a wrong assumption about what's being asked, an incorrect premise) tends to get reinforced rather than caught, because every subsequent token is generated to be locally coherent with everything already written -- including the model's own mistakes. This is also precisely why techniques like asking a model to 'think step by step' measurably help on harder reasoning problems: they don't add a planning module, but they do give the model a place to generate explicit intermediate tokens that it then gets to condition on when producing the final answer, which is a meaningfully different (and usually better) starting point than jumping straight to a final answer with no intermediate tokens to build on.

sections.heading: Autoregression: Everything Feeds Back In
sections.body:
The term for this mechanism is **autoregressive generation** -- 'auto' because the model's own previous outputs become part of its own future inputs. Every token the model has generated so far in this response, not just your original prompt, is part of 'everything written so far' that conditions the very next prediction. This is why a single different word placed early in a prompt can cascade into a completely different completion: that word doesn't just sit there passively, it shifts the probability distribution at every single subsequent generation step, and each of those shifted choices then itself becomes part of the conditioning context for the step after that -- small differences compound across the length of the response rather than staying isolated.

As an engineering detail worth knowing (though not required to reason correctly about model behavior): because the sequence only ever grows by one token at a time and the earlier tokens' internal representations don't change, production inference systems use an optimization called a **KV cache** to avoid recomputing attention over the entire prefix from scratch at every single step -- they cache the intermediate results for tokens already processed and only compute the new work for the newest token. This is purely a performance optimization; it doesn't change anything about what gets generated, only how fast it can be computed, but it's worth recognizing the term if you ever see it in an inference framework's documentation or a discussion of generation latency.

examples.title: The Autoregressive Loop, Made Explicit
examples.explanation: This is, mechanically, what happens underneath every call to a hosted chat completion API -- the API just does this loop for you, server-side, and hides the per-token detail behind a single request/response. Two lines matter most. `logits = model.forward(tokens)` recomputes a full forward pass over the *entire* sequence so far, including every previously generated token -- not just the original prompt -- which is exactly the autoregressive property: the model's own output has become part of its own input. And `tokens.append(next_token)` is what makes the loop actually make progress -- forgetting this line (or resetting `tokens` each iteration) is a real bug you can introduce by hand and is exactly the subject of the debugging exercise below. Note also that `model.forward(tokens)` returns logits for every position in the sequence, and we only care about `logits[-1]` -- the distribution for the token that comes after everything currently in `tokens`.

examples.title: One Changed Word, a Different Trajectory
examples.code:
prompt_a = "Write one sentence about the weather. It was a sunny day, so"
prompt_b = "Write one sentence about the weather. It was a stormy day, so"

# Both prompts are identical except for one adjective. Because every subsequent
# token is generated conditioned on everything before it, that single word
# shifts the probability distribution at EVERY later generation step, not just
# the very next one -- the two completions typically diverge completely:
#
# prompt_a -> "...everyone decided to go for a walk in the park."
# prompt_b -> "...everyone decided to stay inside and wait it out."
examples.explanation: Nothing here is a special case or an unusual prompting trick -- it's the direct, expected consequence of autoregressive conditioning. The word 'sunny' versus 'stormy' changes the probability distribution over the very next token (what plausibly follows 'so' after a sunny versus stormy setup), and whichever token actually gets chosen then becomes part of the input for predicting the token after that, and so on. There's no mechanism by which the two completions could be expected to reconverge or stay similar once they've diverged -- each new token is generated fresh from whatever the sequence currently contains, with no memory of 'what the prompt would have implied under the other wording.' This is exactly why small, seemingly cosmetic changes to a prompt -- word choice, order, an extra clarifying clause -- can produce disproportionately different outputs, and why prompt changes should always be evaluated empirically rather than assumed to be equivalent because they 'mean basically the same thing' to a human reader.

examples.title: A Wrong Token Gets Reinforced, Not Caught
examples.code:
prompt = "The Eiffel Tower was completed in the year"

# Suppose the model's next-token step, for whatever reason, assigns the
# highest probability to an incorrect year token, e.g. "1832" instead of
# the correct 1889. Once that token is emitted and appended:
#
# "The Eiffel Tower was completed in the year 1832, during a period of
#  rapid industrial expansion in France..."
#
# Every token after "1832" is generated to be a PLAUSIBLE, FLUENT
# continuation of a sentence that already contains "1832" -- there is no
# step where the model reconsiders whether 1832 was correct in the first place.
examples.explanation: This illustrates one of the most important practical consequences of having no explicit planning or self-correction phase: once a token is committed -- right or wrong -- it becomes a permanent, unquestioned part of the context that every future token is conditioned on. The model isn't 'lying' or being deceptive when it builds a fluent, confident-sounding sentence around an incorrect year; it's doing exactly what next-token prediction always does, which is produce a locally plausible continuation of exactly the text that currently exists, including its own earlier mistake. This is the generation-mechanism half of why hallucinations tend to read as fluent and self-consistent rather than hedged or self-doubting -- there's no mechanism in the basic generation loop that would make the model pause and re-examine an earlier claim. The next concept covers the other half of this story: why the wrong token got the highest probability in the first place.

misconceptions.description: The model plans out the overall structure or argument of its response before it starts generating, the way a person might sketch an outline before writing.
misconceptions.clarification: There is no separate planning phase anywhere in the base generation mechanism -- every token, including the first one, is produced by the same next-token-prediction step conditioned only on the text that already exists. Apparent planning is an emergent side effect of the model having learned, from massive amounts of training text, what token sequences that eventually turn out coherent tend to look like early on -- not evidence of a distinct planning module. This is also precisely why explicitly prompting a model to write out intermediate reasoning ('think step by step') before its final answer measurably helps on harder problems: it doesn't invoke a hidden planning mechanism, it gives the model real, explicit tokens to condition later generation on, which a jump-straight-to-the-answer response never had.

misconceptions.description: If a model states something factually wrong partway through a response, it will typically notice and correct itself later in the same response, the way a careful person catches their own mistake mid-sentence.
misconceptions.clarification: The base autoregressive loop has no built-in mechanism that revisits or re-evaluates earlier tokens once they've been generated -- each new token is produced to be a plausible continuation of everything already written, including any earlier errors, which tends to reinforce a mistake with fluent, consistent-sounding surrounding text rather than flag or fix it. Self-correction only happens when it's explicitly engineered in some other way -- for instance, a separate verification pass, a tool call that checks a claim, or a prompting strategy that asks the model to critique its own draft as a distinct subsequent step -- never as a default property of generating one continuous response.

exercises.prompt: This simplified generation loop has a bug. What will actually happen when generate() is called -- will it produce a normal-looking multi-token response, get stuck, or something else? Explain why.
exercises.code:
def generate(prompt_tokens, model, max_new_tokens=20, eos_token_id=50256):
    tokens = list(prompt_tokens)
    output = []
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        logits = model.forward(tokens)     # NOTE: always forwards the ORIGINAL tokens
        probs = softmax(logits[-1])
        next_token = argmax(probs)
        if next_token == eos_token_id:
            break
        output.append(next_token)
    return output
hints: Compare this loop carefully to the correct version shown in the explanation -- what happens to the `tokens` list across iterations here versus there?
`model.forward(tokens)` is always called with the exact same `tokens` list. Does anything in this loop body ever add the newly generated token back into `tokens`?
If the input to the model never changes between iterations, what would you expect the model's output -- the highest-probability next token -- to do between iterations?
exercises.expectedAnswer: The loop will very likely produce the same token repeated max_new_tokens times (or get stuck generating the same token until the loop limit is hit), because `tokens` never gets the newly generated token appended to it -- every iteration calls model.forward on the exact same, unchanging prompt_tokens, so the model computes the exact same probability distribution and greedily picks the exact same highest-probability token every single time.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is that `next_token` is appended to `output` but never appended back to `tokens`, which is what gets fed into `model.forward()` on the next iteration. Since `tokens` is identical on every pass through the loop, and greedy decoding (`argmax`) is deterministic, the model computes the exact same logits and therefore picks the exact same token every single time -- the loop doesn't crash, but it produces a degenerate, repeated-token output instead of a coherent continuation. This is a very direct illustration of why autoregression matters mechanically, not just conceptually: forgetting to feed the model's own output back in as input isn't a cosmetic bug, it removes the entire mechanism that lets generation make forward progress at all.

exercises.prompt: A team's custom local-inference wrapper around an open-weights model produces oddly repetitive output -- long stretches of the same word or phrase repeated over and over. Find the bug in this generation loop and fix it.
hints: Look closely at what variable gets passed into `model.forward()` each time through the loop, versus what variable actually accumulates the newly generated tokens.
`tokens` is being correctly appended to at the bottom of the loop -- but is `tokens` the thing actually being fed back into the model on the next pass?
The fix is a one-variable-name change: the model needs to see its own previously generated tokens as part of its input on every subsequent call.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The loop correctly appends each new token to `tokens`, but the call to `model.forward()` was passing `prompt_tokens` -- the original, never-updated prompt -- instead of `tokens`, the list that actually grows as generation proceeds. As a result, the model was being asked, over and over, 'what comes right after the original prompt,' with no awareness that it had already generated several tokens past that point -- so it kept regenerating whatever token it considered most probable immediately after the prompt, producing exactly the repetitive-loop symptom described. Swapping `prompt_tokens` for `tokens` in the `forward()` call restores the autoregressive property: each step now correctly conditions on the full sequence generated so far, not just the original input.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following best describes how an LLM decides the very next token to output at a given point in generation?
options: It looks up the most grammatically correct next word using a rule-based grammar engine trained alongside the model.
It computes a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary, conditioned on all tokens generated so far (prompt plus its own prior output), and selects a token from that distribution.
It retrieves the most similar sentence from its training data and copies the next word from that sentence.
It first generates a short outline of the intended response, then fills in each token to match that outline.
assessments.explanation: This is the core autoregressive mechanism: a forward pass produces one logit per vocabulary entry, softmax converts those into a probability distribution, and a token is selected from it -- with the entire process conditioned on every token that already exists in the sequence, including tokens the model itself generated earlier in the same response. Option A is wrong because there's no separate symbolic grammar engine involved; grammatical patterns are represented implicitly in the learned probability distribution. Option C is wrong because the model doesn't perform a literal lookup or retrieval against stored training sentences at generation time -- it generates from learned parameters, not a searchable copy of its training data. Option D is wrong because there's no distinct planning/outlining phase in the base mechanism; any apparent structure emerges from token-by-token prediction alone, unless an explicit intermediate-reasoning step is added through prompting.

assessments.prompt: Explain, strictly in terms of the autoregressive next-token-prediction mechanism, why explicitly asking a model to 'think step by step' before giving its final answer often improves accuracy on multi-step reasoning problems.
assessments.modelAnswer: Every token a model generates is produced by conditioning on everything already in the sequence -- the prompt plus every token it has generated so far in this response -- and there is no separate mechanism that lets the model 'work something out internally' without that work existing as actual generated tokens somewhere in the sequence. If you ask a multi-step reasoning question and demand only a final answer, the model has to produce that answer as essentially the very next token(s), conditioned on nothing but the question itself -- there's no intermediate scratch space, because nothing in the base mechanism provides one. Asking the model to 'think step by step' changes what actually gets generated before the final answer: the model now produces explicit intermediate tokens -- restating the problem, working through sub-steps, computing intermediate quantities -- and, crucially, every one of those intermediate tokens becomes part of the context that the eventual final-answer tokens are conditioned on. In effect, you're not invoking a hidden reasoning module; you're using the exact same next-token-prediction mechanism to generate a scratchpad, and then letting the model condition its final answer on that scratchpad instead of jumping straight from 'here's the question' to 'here's the answer' with nothing in between. Because next-token prediction is demonstrably better at producing a locally plausible next step when there's relevant, explicit context to build on, giving the model its own worked intermediate steps to condition on tends to produce a more accurate final answer than forcing the entire multi-step problem to be solved implicitly in the single leap straight to a final answer.

assessments.prompt: At each step of the generation loop, what exactly does the model's final layer compute before a next token is chosen?
options: One logit per vocabulary entry, which softmax then converts into a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary that sums to 1.
A single probability value representing how confident the model is in its overall response so far.
A ranked shortlist of the five most likely next words, computed by comparing against stored training sentences.
A binary flag for every vocabulary entry indicating whether that token is grammatically valid at this position.
assessments.explanation: The model produces one real-valued logit per vocabulary entry -- tens of thousands of numbers -- and softmax converts that full set of logits into a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary that sums to exactly 1. Option B is wrong because there is no single scalar 'overall confidence' computed at each step, only a distribution over the next token. Option C is wrong because generation doesn't work by comparing against stored training sentences at inference time. Option D is wrong because there's no separate binary grammar-validity check; grammaticality is implicitly reflected in the learned logit values themselves, not a distinct pass/fail flag.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the ways the basic autoregressive generation loop actually terminates, according to this module?
options: The model generates a special end-of-sequence token it has learned marks the response as complete.
The response reaches a configured maximum-length limit.
The generated text matches a configured stop sequence.
The model internally recognizes it has 'sufficiently answered' the question and raises a distinct completion signal separate from any generated token.
assessments.explanation: The module lists exactly three termination conditions: an end-of-sequence token, a max-length limit, and a matched stop sequence -- all of which are either tokens the model generates or external configuration you set. Option D describes a mechanism that does not exist in the base loop: there is no separate internal 'I'm done' signal distinct from the actual tokens produced -- the loop only ever stops because of one of the three concrete, token-or-config-based conditions.

assessments.prompt: Two prompts are identical except that one early word differs ('sunny' vs. 'stormy'), yet their multi-sentence completions end up completely different, not just different in that one spot. What mechanism explains why the difference cascades rather than staying local?
options: The model re-plans and rewrites the entire response from scratch whenever any single input word changes.

Each generated token is conditioned on every token that precedes it, including the model's own prior output, so a shifted choice at one step alters the input to every later step, and those differences compound across the response.
Different adjectives route the prompt to different hard-coded response templates stored in the model's weights.
The tokenizer assigns a different total token budget depending on which adjective is used, changing how much room is left for the response.
assessments.explanation: Autoregressive generation conditions every new token on the entire sequence so far, including tokens the model itself already generated in this response. A different early word shifts the probability distribution at the very next step; whichever token actually gets picked then becomes part of the context for the step after that, and so on -- so a small initial difference compounds rather than staying isolated. There's no re-planning phase (option A), no template-routing mechanism (option C), and adjective choice doesn't change the token budget in the way option D describes.

concepts.title: Sampling, Temperature, and Why Models Hallucinate
concepts.description: Temperature and sampling strategy control how a model turns its next-token probability distribution into an actual chosen token -- and that same probabilistic mechanism, not a database lookup or a fact-checking step, is the root cause of hallucination, which is why no amount of sampling-parameter tuning alone can eliminate it.
learningObjectives: Explain what the temperature parameter does mathematically to a next-token probability distribution, and predict its qualitative effect at low, moderate, and high settings.
Compare greedy decoding, temperature sampling, and top-p (nucleus) sampling, and choose an appropriate strategy for a given use case.
Explain why hallucination is an expected consequence of the training objective and generation mechanism rather than a rare software defect.
Explain why temperature 0 (greedy decoding) reduces output variance but does not reduce hallucination rate.
Identify concrete hallucination mitigation strategies and articulate why each one reduces, but cannot fully eliminate, the underlying risk.

sections.heading: What Temperature Actually Does to the Distribution
sections.body:
Recall from the previous concept that the model's final layer produces one logit per vocabulary token, and softmax converts those logits into a probability distribution. **Temperature** is a single number that gets applied just before that softmax step: every logit is divided by the temperature value before the softmax conversion happens.

The effect of that simple division is not intuitive on first encounter, so it's worth reasoning through directly. Dividing by a temperature **less than 1** makes the differences between logits relatively *larger*, which softmax then converts into a *more sharply peaked* distribution -- the already-most-probable tokens become even more dominant, and the model's choices become more consistent and more deterministic across repeated calls. Dividing by a temperature **greater than 1** does the opposite: it shrinks the relative differences between logits, flattening the distribution, and giving tokens that were only moderately probable a meaningfully better chance of being selected -- producing more varied, sometimes more creative, and also more erratic output. **Temperature exactly 0** is a special-cased limit rather than a literal division (dividing by zero is undefined) -- essentially every production API treats temperature 0 as 'skip sampling entirely, always pick the single highest-probability token,' which is exactly greedy decoding.

```python
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "List three uses for a paperclip."}],
    temperature=0.2,   # sharply peaked: consistent, conservative, low variety across calls
)
```

A useful mental model: temperature doesn't change what the model 'believes' is most probable -- it only changes how strictly the actual token selection sticks to that belief versus how much it explores less-probable alternatives.

sections.heading: Beyond Temperature: Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling
sections.body:
Temperature alone reshapes the whole distribution, but it doesn't remove the long tail of genuinely implausible tokens -- at a high enough temperature, even a token with a tiny original probability retains some nonzero chance of being selected. Two additional, commonly combined techniques address this directly by restricting *which* tokens are even eligible for selection before temperature and sampling are applied.

**Top-k sampling** restricts the candidate pool to only the k highest-probability tokens (say, the top 40), then samples from just that restricted pool. This is simple but has an awkward property: a fixed k is sometimes too restrictive (when the distribution is naturally flat and spread across many reasonable options) and sometimes too permissive (when the distribution is naturally sharp and only two or three tokens are genuinely plausible, but k=40 still lets clearly-bad options into the pool).

**Top-p sampling** (also called **nucleus sampling**) fixes exactly that problem by making the pool size adaptive: instead of a fixed count, it includes the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose cumulative probability just exceeds some threshold p (commonly around 0.9 or 0.95). When the model is very confident and the distribution is sharply peaked, the nucleus might contain only two or three tokens; when the model is genuinely uncertain and the distribution is spread out, the nucleus naturally grows to include more candidates. This adaptivity is why top-p is generally preferred over a fixed top-k in production systems, and why many APIs let you set both temperature and top_p together -- they're complementary, not redundant: top_p decides the eligible pool, and temperature reshapes how sharply probability is distributed within that pool.

sections.heading: Hallucination Is the Mechanism Working as Designed, Not a Bug
sections.body:
This is the single most important reframing to internalize about hallucination: the model was trained to predict plausible, fluent continuations of text, not to assert only independently-verified facts -- and there is no separate module anywhere in the architecture that checks a generated claim against ground truth before it gets emitted. At the moment of generating any specific token, the model has no distinct internal signal marking 'this token is something I've verified is true' versus 'this token is simply the most locally plausible continuation of everything written so far.' Both a correct fact and a fabricated one come out of the exact same probability distribution, computed by the exact same mechanism.

This is why hallucinated content so often reads as every bit as fluent, confident, and well-structured as correct content -- there is nothing in the generation process that would mark a fabrication differently from a verified statement, because fluency and plausibility (not calibrated truthfulness) are what the underlying training objective actually optimized for. A model that has genuinely learned a fact well (because it appeared frequently, consistently, and unambiguously across its training data) will tend to reproduce it reliably, for the mundane reason that doing so really is the highest-probability continuation. A model asked about something rare, ambiguous, contradictory across its training sources, or simply outside what it was ever trained on will still produce *a* highest-probability continuation -- fluent, grammatically confident, formatted just like a correct answer would be -- because generating *something* plausible-sounding is what the mechanism does, unconditionally, every single time it's asked to produce a next token.

sections.heading: Why Temperature 0 Doesn't Fix It
sections.body:
A very common, very reasonable-sounding intuition is that setting temperature to 0 should make the model 'more careful' or 'more truthful,' since it removes randomness. It's important to be precise about what temperature 0 actually changes: it removes *sampling variance* -- the model will now deterministically pick the single highest-probability token at every step, every single time you ask, rather than occasionally sampling a different one. What it does **not** change is which token the model considers most probable in the first place.

If the model's learned distribution happens to assign the highest probability to an incorrect fact -- a plausible-sounding but wrong function signature, a fabricated citation, an incorrect date -- greedy decoding will produce that exact same wrong answer with total consistency, every time you ask, with no variance at all. Temperature 0 trades away the chance of an occasionally-different (and possibly occasionally-correct) sampled alternative in exchange for perfect determinism around whatever the model's single most-probable guess happens to be, right or wrong. Raising temperature, meanwhile, doesn't reliably fix hallucination either -- it increases the chance of sampling from the tail of the distribution, which can just as easily introduce a *new*, different fabrication as it can surface a better answer. There is no dial here that trades cleanly between 'more deterministic' and 'more truthful' -- determinism and correctness are simply different, largely unrelated axes.

sections.heading: Mitigations and Their Real Limits
sections.body: None of the following make hallucination structurally impossible, because none of them change the underlying probabilistic generation mechanism -- but each meaningfully reduces its likelihood or its blast radius, which is why real systems typically combine several of them. **Grounding via retrieval** (the subject of the next module) narrows the plausible-continuation space by injecting relevant, verified text directly into the context, so the highest-probability continuation is far more likely to actually match that provided material -- this is empirically the single most effective lever available today. **Lowering temperature** reduces run-to-run variance, which is useful for consistency and reproducibility, but as covered above, does not by itself improve correctness. **Asking for citations or sources** can help, but only if you actually verify that the cited source exists and says what's claimed -- a model can hallucinate a fake citation with exactly the same fluent confidence it hallucinates any other claim, so an unverified citation is not evidence of anything. **Structured verification passes** -- asking the model to quote the exact span of a source it's relying on, or running a second, independent pass that checks a claim against retrieved evidence -- add real cost and latency but meaningfully catch cases the first pass got wrong. The honest, non-negotiable limit underneath all of this: as long as generation is a single probabilistic mechanism that produces correct and incorrect statements through the identical process, no purely generative technique reduces hallucination risk to zero -- for any use case where being wrong is costly, some form of external verification or grounding is not optional polish, it's a requirement.

examples.title: The Same Prompt at Three Temperatures
examples.code:
prompt = "Suggest a name for a new coffee shop."

for temp in [0.0, 0.7, 1.3]:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        temperature=temp,
    )
    print(temp, "->", response.choices[0].message.content)

# temp=0.0 -> "The Daily Grind"          (same answer basically every run)
# temp=0.7 -> "Brew & Co."                (varies moderately across runs)
# temp=1.3 -> "Percolate Dreams Cafe"     (more varied, occasionally odd, across runs)
examples.explanation: At temperature 0, the distribution collapses to greedy selection of whatever the model considers the single most probable name -- run this many times and you'll get the same or nearly the same answer nearly every time, because there's no sampling randomness left to produce variety. At a moderate temperature like 0.7, the distribution still favors likely candidates but leaves enough probability mass on other reasonable options that repeated calls genuinely explore different, still-sensible names. At a high temperature like 1.3, the distribution is flattened enough that lower-probability, more unusual tokens get selected more often, which can read as more 'creative' but can just as easily drift into names that are slightly incoherent or off-brief -- there's no guarantee that flattening the distribution only surfaces *good* unlikely options rather than *bad* ones. This is exactly why creative-writing or brainstorming features tend to use higher temperatures, while factual Q&A, classification, or code-generation features tend to use low or zero temperature -- not because low temperature makes answers more correct, but because it makes them more consistent, which matters more when variety itself isn't the goal.

examples.title: Greedy Decoding Still Hallucinates, Consistently
examples.code:
prompt = "What year was the Python programming language first released, and by whom?"

for _ in range(3):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="some-model",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        temperature=0.0,
    )
    print(response.choices[0].message.content)

# Suppose, hypothetically, a weaker or older model's most-probable answer here
# were subtly wrong -- e.g. citing the wrong year or the wrong original author.
# At temperature 0.0, all three calls would return that SAME wrong answer,
# with identical confident phrasing every single time.
examples.explanation: This example is intentionally about the *shape* of the failure, not a specific real model's actual accuracy on this particular fact. The point is structural: if a model's learned distribution places the highest probability on an incorrect answer -- for any reason, including ambiguous or sparse training signal -- temperature 0 does not give the model any additional chance to reconsider or land on a different, possibly correct, answer; it deterministically reproduces that single highest-probability output every time. This is exactly why 'the model gave me the same wrong answer three times in a row' should never be read as corroborating evidence of correctness -- consistency at temperature 0 reflects the determinism of greedy decoding, not independent confirmation of the claim. Verifying a factual claim requires checking it against an actual source, not asking the same deterministic model the same question again.

examples.title: Top-p Adapting to How Peaked the Distribution Is
examples.code:
# Step where the next token is nearly certain -- e.g. completing "Thank you very"
# The distribution might be: {"much": 0.94, "kindly": 0.03, ...tiny tail...}
# With top_p=0.9, the nucleus contains essentially just "much" -- barely any
# alternative gets included, because one token alone already exceeds 0.9.

# Step where many continuations are genuinely reasonable -- e.g. completing
# "My favorite hobby is"
# The distribution might be spread across many options: {"reading": 0.12,
# "hiking": 0.10, "cooking": 0.09, "painting": 0.07, ...many more...}
# With the same top_p=0.9, the nucleus now has to include many more tokens
# before their cumulative probability crosses 0.9.

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "My favorite hobby is"}],
    top_p=0.9,
    temperature=0.8,
)
examples.explanation: The core advantage of top-p over a fixed top-k shows up exactly in this contrast: the same top_p=0.9 setting produces a tiny, almost-certain nucleus at the first (nearly-deterministic) step, and a much larger, genuinely varied nucleus at the second (genuinely open-ended) step -- because the pool boundary is defined by cumulative probability, not a fixed count of tokens. A fixed top-k=40, by contrast, would force the model to consider 40 candidate tokens at the first step too, even though only one or two are remotely reasonable there, needlessly leaving the door open to a clearly wrong completion of 'Thank you very' that a human would never produce. This adaptivity is precisely why top-p is the more common default in production sampling configurations -- it tracks the model's own confidence at each individual step, rather than applying one fixed rule everywhere regardless of how sharp or flat that particular step's distribution actually is.

misconceptions.description: Setting temperature to 0 makes the model 'more careful,' 'more honest,' or otherwise more likely to be factually correct.
misconceptions.clarification: Temperature 0 only removes sampling randomness -- it forces the model to always pick the single highest-probability token at every step (greedy decoding) rather than sometimes sampling a different one. It does not change which token the model's learned parameters consider most probable in the first place. If that highest-probability answer happens to be wrong, temperature 0 will reproduce that exact same wrong answer with total consistency every time you ask, rather than occasionally landing on a different, possibly correct, alternative. Determinism and correctness are different, largely independent properties -- temperature controls the former, not the latter.

misconceptions.description: When a model states something false, it's because it 'doesn't know' the answer, and if it truly didn't know, it would say so or express uncertainty, the way a person would.
misconceptions.clarification: The model has no separate internal signal at generation time that distinguishes 'a fact I've reliably learned' from 'the most locally plausible-sounding continuation, regardless of whether it's actually true' -- both come from exactly the same probability distribution, produced by exactly the same mechanism. Hedging or expressing uncertainty is not a default, automatic behavior that kicks in when the model 'doesn't know' something; it only happens when the training data or prompting conditions the model to produce hedging language in that specific situation. Fluent, confident phrasing is therefore not evidence that a claim is correct -- confidence-sounding tone and factual accuracy are simply not linked by the generation mechanism at all.

exercises.prompt: The same prompt is sent to a chat completion API twice at temperature=0.0, and separately, twice at temperature=1.2. Predict whether each pair of calls is likely to return identical text, and explain the difference between the two pairs.
exercises.code:
for _ in range(2):
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name a color."}],
        temperature=0.0,
    )
    print("temp=0.0:", r.choices[0].message.content)

for _ in range(2):
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name a color."}],
        temperature=1.2,
    )
    print("temp=1.2:", r.choices[0].message.content)
hints: Temperature 0 is treated as a special case by most APIs -- what sampling behavior does it collapse down to?
At a high temperature, the distribution over next tokens is flattened, giving lower-probability tokens a real chance of being selected -- does that make repeated calls more or less likely to agree?

Note: some providers' infrastructure introduces tiny amounts of nondeterminism even at temperature 0 for performance reasons, so 'identical' in practice sometimes means 'nearly always identical' rather than a hard mathematical guarantee -- but the qualitative contrast between the two settings should still hold.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The two temperature=0.0 calls are very likely to return the same color both times, because temperature 0 collapses to greedy decoding -- always selecting the single highest-probability token deterministically. The two temperature=1.2 calls are much more likely to return different colors, because the flattened distribution at high temperature gives multiple plausible colors a real, differing chance of being sampled on each independent call.
exercises.solutionExplanation: At temperature 0.0, softmax's sharpening behavior (or the special-cased greedy shortcut most APIs implement directly) means the model deterministically returns whatever single token it considers most probable at each generation step -- with no randomness in the selection process, repeated identical calls should return the same or nearly the same output. At temperature 1.2, the distribution is deliberately flattened, spreading meaningful probability across several plausible colors rather than concentrating it on just one -- so each call performs an independent random draw from that broader set, and two separate draws landing on the same color becomes far less certain. This exercise is really testing the same underlying fact from the explanation: temperature governs how much randomness enters the selection process, not what the model 'believes,' which is exactly why it affects consistency but not correctness.

exercises.prompt: A customer-support bot is fabricating specific policy details (wrong refund windows, invented exceptions) that don't match the company's actual, real policy. The team's first fix attempt was to set temperature to 0, reasoning that this would make the bot 'stick to the facts.' The hallucinations continued at the same rate. Diagnose why this fix didn't work, and propose one that actually addresses the root cause.
exercises.code:
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful customer support assistant. Answer accurately."},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_question},
    ],
    temperature=0.0,   # the team's attempted fix
)
hints: What does temperature actually control -- the model's underlying beliefs about what's probable, or only how deterministically it acts on those beliefs?
The system message says 'answer accurately,' but does the model actually have access to the company's real, current policy anywhere in this request?
Without the real policy text present in the context somewhere, what is the model's 'most probable continuation' actually based on?
exercises.solutionCode:
policy_chunks = retrieve_relevant_policy(user_question)   # e.g. from a vector index of the real policy docs
context_text = "\n\n".join(policy_chunks)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": (
            "You are a customer support assistant. Answer ONLY using the policy "
            "excerpts provided below. If the answer isn't contained in the excerpts, "
            "say you don't know and offer to escalate to a human.\n\n"
            f"Policy excerpts:\n{context_text}"
        )},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_question},
    ],
    temperature=0.0,
)
exercises.solutionExplanation: Temperature only controls how deterministically the model acts on its existing probability distribution -- it has no effect on what that distribution actually contains, and the original request never gave the model the real policy text at all, just an instruction to 'answer accurately' with nothing to be accurate *from*. Asking a model to be accurate about content it was never shown is asking the generation mechanism to do something it structurally cannot do: with no grounding text present, the model's highest-probability continuation is just whatever generic, plausible-sounding policy language its training data makes likely, regardless of temperature. The real fix is grounding: retrieve the actual, current policy text relevant to the question and include it directly in the prompt, with an explicit instruction to answer only from that provided text (and to say so, rather than guess, if the answer isn't present). This doesn't make hallucination impossible, but it gives the model something true to condition on, which is the mechanism that actually reduces fabrication -- temperature was never the relevant lever for this particular failure.

assessments.prompt: Setting a model's temperature parameter to 0 primarily has which effect?
options: It makes the model check its answer against external sources before responding.
It forces the model to always select the single highest-probability token at each step (greedy decoding), removing sampling randomness but not changing which token is most probable.
It reduces the model's vocabulary to only the most common, 'safe' words.
It guarantees the model will express uncertainty whenever it is unsure of an answer.
assessments.explanation: Temperature 0 is the special-cased limit where sampling is replaced entirely by always picking the argmax (highest-probability) token, making output deterministic across repeated identical calls -- but it does nothing to the underlying probabilities the model computed, so an incorrect highest-probability answer stays incorrect and is simply reproduced consistently. Option A describes a feature no temperature setting provides on its own -- verification requires a separate, explicit step like retrieval or a check pass. Option C is wrong because temperature reshapes the probability distribution over the existing vocabulary; it doesn't remove or restrict which words exist in that vocabulary. Option D is wrong because expressing uncertainty is not an automatic behavior triggered by any sampling setting -- it only happens if the model has actually learned to produce hedging language in that situation, which temperature has no influence over.

assessments.prompt: A colleague argues: 'if the model can hallucinate a wrong fact with the exact same fluent, confident tone as a correct one, how are users supposed to trust anything it says?' Explain why this happens in terms of the generation mechanism, and what it implies for how you should design a product that surfaces LLM output directly to end users.
assessments.modelAnswer: This happens because fluency and factual correctness are not linked anywhere in the generation mechanism -- every token, whether it happens to state a verified fact or a fabricated one, is produced by the exact same next-token-prediction process, drawing from a probability distribution shaped by what's statistically plausible given the training data and the current context, not by any distinct internal check against ground truth. The model has no separate 'confidence I've verified this' signal that would make correct statements sound different from incorrect ones; a hallucinated claim gets the same grammatical structure, the same assertive phrasing, and the same overall tone as a true one, because both are generated by the identical mechanism optimizing for the same thing: a locally plausible continuation of the text so far.
