The practical implication for product design is significant: you cannot rely on the model's own tone or phrasing as a signal of reliability, and you should design as if every output requires either grounding, verification, or an explicit acknowledgment of uncertainty to the end user, rather than assuming fluent output implies correct output. Concretely, this pushes toward architectural choices like retrieval-augmented generation for anything factual (so claims are at least traceable to a real source you can show or check), explicit citations that a human or a separate process actually verifies rather than trusting blindly, UI patterns that make it clear to users when content is AI-generated and not independently verified, and reserving unguarded, ungrounded generation for genuinely low-stakes use cases (brainstorming, creative drafts) where an occasional plausible-but-wrong output causes no real harm. The underlying lesson is that trustworthiness has to be engineered in from outside the generation mechanism -- it is not something you can extract from the model's own output by reading its tone.

assessments.prompt: How does top-p (nucleus) sampling decide which tokens are eligible for selection, and how does that differ from top-k sampling?
options: Top-p includes the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold, so the pool size adapts to how peaked or flat the distribution is at each step; top-k always uses a fixed candidate count regardless of the distribution's shape.
Top-p and top-k are two names for the exact same mechanism, differing only in which APIs expose which name.
Top-p selects tokens alphabetically from among the top-k highest-probability candidates.
Top-p is only applied when temperature is set to 0, while top-k is only applied at nonzero temperature.
assessments.explanation: Top-p's pool boundary is defined by cumulative probability crossing a threshold p, so a sharply peaked distribution yields a tiny nucleus and a flat distribution yields a larger one -- it adapts per step. Top-k, by contrast, always considers exactly k candidates no matter how peaked or flat the actual distribution is, which is precisely the limitation top-p was designed to fix. Options B, C, and D all misstate the mechanisms: they are distinct techniques, neither is alphabetical, and neither is gated on a specific temperature value.

assessments.prompt: Which statement about hallucination mitigation strategies best matches this module's discussion of their real limits?
options: Grounding via retrieval eliminates hallucination entirely, since a grounded model can only ever repeat the retrieved text verbatim.
Asking the model to provide citations is sufficient on its own, since a model that fabricates facts will not also fabricate a citation.

Retrieval meaningfully reduces hallucination risk by narrowing the space of plausible continuations, but no purely generative technique drives that risk to zero, so verification remains necessary for high-stakes use cases.
Setting temperature to 0 is the most effective mitigation, since it removes the sampling randomness that causes hallucination.
assessments.explanation: The module is explicit that grounding via retrieval is the most effective lever available but does not make hallucination structurally impossible, because it doesn't change the underlying probabilistic generation mechanism -- some form of external verification remains non-optional wherever being wrong is costly. Option A overstates retrieval's guarantee. Option B is directly contradicted by the module's point that a model can hallucinate a fake citation just as fluently as any other claim. Option D is wrong because temperature only affects sampling variance, not which answer the model considers most probable, so it doesn't reduce hallucination rate.

assessments.prompt: Why do hallucinated statements typically come out just as fluent and confident-sounding as accurate ones, rather than hedged or tentative?
options: A dedicated confidence-estimation module miscalibrates specifically on false statements, making them sound artificially confident.

Both correct and fabricated tokens are produced by the identical next-token-prediction mechanism optimizing for locally plausible continuation, and there is no internal signal at generation time distinguishing a verified fact from a plausible-sounding fabrication.
Models are explicitly trained with a reward signal that punishes hedging language regardless of correctness.
Hedging phrases are removed from the vocabulary by default and must be manually re-enabled through a configuration flag.
assessments.explanation: The module's core reframing is that hallucination is the generation mechanism working as designed, not a distinct malfunction: every token, true or fabricated, is produced by the same probability distribution optimizing for plausible continuation, with no separate 'this is verified' marker anywhere in the process. Hedging only appears when training data or prompting conditions the model to produce it in that specific situation -- it isn't a default reaction to low confidence. Options A, C, and D each invent a mechanism (a confidence estimator, an anti-hedging reward, a disabled vocabulary subset) that the module never describes as part of how these models actually work.
